transcript:
>> Live from NPR News, I'm Charles Snyder.
President Trump is due back at the White House after speaking in Oklahoma Thursday night
as part of a stepped up travel schedule ahead of next month's midterm elections.
The president campaigning for GOP candidates even as his approval remains firmly below
40% by most polls.
Here's NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben.
>> Trump's speech, which lasted nearly an hour and a half, covered familiar ground like
promoting Republican tax cuts and baselessly accusing Democrats of cheating in elections.
Friday, Trump will travel to deep red Alabama to speak, and Saturday he is scheduled to
speak in Ohio.
That state, which has turned redder in recent years, has tight Senate and governor's races
this year.
When asked by a reporter today why he's campaigning in solidly Republican states like Oklahoma,
he responded, quote, I won all of them by a lot.
I'm going there just to make sure.
>> He added that he wanted to thank Oklahoma for voting for him in three presidential elections.
Danielle Kurtzleben, NPR News.
>> Attorneys for Tennessee death row in May Krista Pike say Pike is still alive but in
critical condition.
They spoke to reporters Thursday after the state's failed attempt to execute Pike by
lethal injection for a 1995 murder when she was 18.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee calling what happened deeply disturbing and has ordered an independent
review.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed Attorney General Letitia James as a special
prosecutor in the alleged gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024.
In a statement, Hochul said she is turning to a special prosecutor because she has lost
faith in local district attorney Matthew Van Houten's ability to handle the case.
Embarrassed Brian Mann, Zach Cornell, and it's more on what Van Houten is saying.
>> Van Houten has now suggested in a statement that Cornell campus police didn't give them
all the necessary information from their interviews with the woman.
He says he never saw that statement that she was 100% confident that she was raped.
Here's what Van Houten said in an email to our member station WSKG.
If it's factual, he wrote, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said
to the police.
That was not in her six page statement.
>> Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says the co-pilot accused of sabotaging a Dubai
to Tel Aviv flight is from Oman.
NPR's Kat Lonstorf reports on questions being raised about the pilot vetting process.
>> Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with
to fly into its airspace.
That includes Oman.
Speaking on Fox News, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel checks
the background of pilots flying routes into the country.
He said that this pilot must have gotten through a, quote, loophole.
Israeli officials have said the incident was an attempted terrorist attack, although the
motive is still unknown.
The United Arab Emirates says it's opened an investigation into what happened on the
flight.
Israel says it's participating in that.
Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and being questioned.
Kat Lonstorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
>> This is NPR.
Federal safety investigators say the pilots of that Amazon cargo plane that crashed in
Miami last month were not warned about the potential for strong tailwinds.
The National Transportation Safety Board released a preliminary report Thursday.
It says an air traffic controller had given a wind advisory to another flight minutes
earlier, but did not inform the Amazon pilots.
The plane landed too fast and overshot the runway, hitting a van and killing five people
inside.
A new federal plan for managing the Colorado River went into effect Thursday.
It forces big cutbacks for three of the states that use its water.
Alex Hager from member station KJZZ reports those states are trying to figure out how they
will bear the pain of those reductions.
>> Arizona is slated to take the biggest cuts under the new rules, but it's close to a deal
with California and Nevada to soften the blow.
State officials say it's hung up while they figure out which specific cities and farms
will use less water.
John Bergrin studies water policy at the nonprofit Western Resource Advocates.
>> That's the real challenge because you're actually talking to people about using less
water and getting cuts.
>> Nevada's decision to sue the federal government over its new plan may have also slowed down
negotiations between the states.
Arizona's top water official says he's very optimistic about the deal, which must be signed
before January 1st.
For NPR News, I'm Alex Hager in Phoenix.
>> The financial markets in Asia are mixed in Friday trading.
Japan's benchmarked EK down 8/10 of a percent.
After stocks edged up on Wall Street, the S&P 500 broke a three-day losing streak.
Mainland Chinese markets are closed for a public holiday.
This is NPR News.
Stay tuned for the following announcements and messages from our sponsors.

topics.text: President Trump campaigns for GOP candidates in Oklahoma ahead of midterm elections
Tennessee execution of death row inmate Krista Pike fails; she remains in critical condition
New York Governor Hochul appoints special prosecutor for alleged Cornell University fraternity rape case
Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu says Dubai to Tel Aviv flight co-pilot accused of sabotage is from Oman
Federal safety investigators say Amazon cargo plane pilots in Miami crash were not warned of tailwinds
New federal plan for Colorado River management forces cutbacks for Arizona, California, and Nevada
Asian financial markets mixed; Japan's Nikkei down, S&P 500 breaks three-day losing streak
